name: Sleep window lock
description: Why: Keep a consistent sleep/wake window. Highest-ROI recovery lever when training is already hard and the job is demanding.
med: Stay within ±30 minutes of target bedtime and wake time
highIntensity: Fixed bedtime, dark/cool room, same wake time including weekends
how:
1) Pick a target bedtime and wake time that yield enough sleep.
2) Set a wind-down alarm 30–45 min before bed.
3) Hold the window weekdays first; expand to weekends when stable.
4) If you miss, shift back by ≤30 min—do not “catch up” with a 2-hour swing.

name: Targeted mobility block
description: Why: Short daily mobility focused on hips, T-spine, and shoulders to offset desk work and heavy training—not another workout.
how:
1) Pick 2–3 problem areas (usually hips, T-spine, shoulders).
2) Set a timer (8–20 min).
3) Slow controlled ranges; breathe; no pain chasing.
4) Do it after wake or before training so it actually happens.

name: Zone-2 / easy recovery
description: Why: Easy aerobic work that aids recovery without competing with hard training sessions.
how:
1) Choose walk, easy bike, or easy jog.
2) Stay conversational pace (roughly Zone 2 / nasal-breathing easy).
3) 25–60 min; stop if it turns into a hard session.
4) Log as recovery, not performance.

name: Stimulant + screen cutoff
description: Why: Protect sleep quality under job stress with caffeine timing and evening wind-down rules.
highIntensity: Full wind-down ritual: no stimulating screens last 60 minutes
how:
1) Hard rule: no caffeine after your cutoff (e.g. 14:00).
2) Last 45–60 min: dim lights, no work chat, no high-stim content.
3) Park phone outside reach or in another room if needed.
4) Replace with low-stim wind-down (stretch, paper book, light tidy).

name: Training auto-reg log
description: Why: Weekly check of sleep, soreness, and motivation; adjust next week’s volume so you don’t grind into injury.
highIntensity: Scores plus explicit volume/intensity adjustment for next week
how:
1) Once a week, score sleep, soreness, and motivation 1–10.
2) If two scores are low, cut volume or intensity next week.
3) Write one sentence: what changes and why.
4) Tell your training plan the decision (calendar note is enough).

name: Protected deep-work block
description: Why: One uninterrupted block on the highest-leverage technical task. Phone away, chat snoozed, single outcome defined before start.
med: 45 minutes, one clear outcome, notifications off
highIntensity: Two 90-minute blocks with a written shutdown between
how:
1) Name one outcome before you start.
2) Kill notifications; phone out of reach.
3) Work one block (45–90 min) without switching tasks.
4) Write a 1-line shutdown: done / next.

name: Weak-skill deliberate practice
description: Why: Focused drill on a known weak skill (system design, algorithm pattern, tool fluency)—not passive content consumption.
med: 25-minute focused drill with one failure mode
highIntensity: 60 minutes plus a feedback artifact (review notes or recorded attempt)
how:
1) Name the weak skill and one failure mode.
2) Drill only that for 25–60 min.
3) Get a feedback signal (tests, review, recording).
4) Note one adjustment for next session.

name: Hard technical reading
description: Why: Read material above comfort level: papers, RFCs, deep chapters—not news or shallow blogs.
highIntensity: Full paper or chapter with written notes
how:
1) Choose material harder than comfort (paper, RFC, deep chapter).
2) Read actively: mark claims you do not yet understand.
3) Write 3–5 bullet notes or a short summary.
4) Queue one idea to apply at work.

name: Spaced system review
description: Why: Short spaced review of notes, flashcards, or system knowledge so job context-switching doesn’t rot skills.
highIntensity: 20 minutes including rewrite of weak cards/notes
how:
1) Open notes or flashcards for 5–20 min.
2) Prioritize weak cards / fuzzy systems.
3) Rewrite anything you cannot explain simply.
4) Stop on the timer—consistency beats marathon reviews.

name: Write-to-clarify
description: Why: Force clarity by writing a decision memo, design note, or explanation. Dual asset for thinking and career.
how:
1) Pick a decision, design, or confusion.
2) Write full sentences (not only bullets) for 15–45 min.
3) State the recommendation or open question at the end.
4) Optionally share or publish the note.

name: High-leverage outreach
description: Why: Send thoughtful outbound messages to people who matter for learning, work, or opportunity—not generic networking spam.
med: One thoughtful message with a clear reason
highIntensity: Three messages including one specific ask
how:
1) Pick one person worth a real connection.
2) Write a specific, human message (why them, why now).
3) Include a light ask or offer when natural.
4) Send—do not draft forever.

name: Relationship CRM pass
description: Why: Weekly scan of key relationships and scheduled next touches. Systems fix the professional habit of forgetting people.
highIntensity: Full list review and calendar next touches
how:
1) Open your short list of important people.
2) Note who you have not touched recently.
3) Send 1–2 nudges or schedule next contact.
4) Capture one line of context for next time.

name: 1:1 outside immediate team
description: Why: Conversation with someone outside your day-to-day team to build weak ties and cross-domain information.
how:
1) Invite someone outside your daily team.
2) Propose a short call or coffee with a clear purpose.
3) Listen more than you pitch.
4) Follow up the same day with one useful note.

name: Same-day follow-up
description: Why: Close open loops the same day: thank-yous, action items, promised intros. Reputation compounder.
med: One follow-up that would otherwise slip
how:
1) At day end (or after each meeting), list open loops.
2) Send thank-yous, action items, or promised intros.
3) Clear or schedule each loop.
4) Do not leave “I’ll do it tomorrow” without a time.

name: Host or contribute in public
description: Why: Show up in a community with real value: useful thread, OSS help, or hosting—not empty networking events.
med: One high-signal public reply or contribution
highIntensity: Run a session or ship meaningful OSS/community help
how:
1) Pick a public surface (thread, OSS, meetup, community).
2) Ship something useful: answer, PR, session, write-up.
3) Optimize for clarity and generosity, not clout.
4) One real contribution beats three passive lurks.

name: Weekly money review
description: Why: Check balances, burn, and runway. Awareness before optimization.
highIntensity: Full personal P&L and runway update
how:
1) Open accounts: cash, burn, big obligations.
2) Note runway / surplus in one line.
3) Flag anything weird (charges, missing transfers).
4) Decide one next action or “no change.”

name: Surplus allocation rule
description: Why: Confirm automated surplus allocation (invest/save). Automation beats weekly willpower.
how:
1) Confirm auto-save/invest transfers ran.
2) If surplus grew, raise rate or rebalance deliberately.
3) Do not re-decide the whole system weekly—execute the rule.
4) Log the check as done.

name: Finance admin batch
description: Why: Batch bills, receipts, and financial inbox so admin drag doesn’t silently accumulate.
how:
1) Open bills, receipts, and finance inbox only.
2) Process for a fixed 15–30 min.
3) Pay, file, or schedule—no browsing other apps.
4) Leave one written next step if unfinished.

name: Compensation / market hygiene
description: Why: Stay calibrated on market rate and compensation levers. Tech careers under-earn without intentionality.
highIntensity: One concrete move: doc ask, negotiation prep, or side-leverage research
how:
1) Note current total comp vs market (even a rough note).
2) Pick one lever: skill, visibility, ask, or side optionality.
3) Do one concrete research or prep action.
4) Schedule the real conversation when ready—not forever “researching.”

name: Targeted spend audit
description: Why: Audit one spend category and cut or renegotiate something real—not generic budgeting theater.
highIntensity: Cut or renegotiate one line item
how:
1) Pick one category (subs, food delivery, tools).
2) Review last 2–4 weeks of spend.
3) Cut, renegotiate, or consciously keep one line.
4) Write the decision so you do not re-litigate weekly.

name: Daily top-3 force rank
description: Why: Name the three outcomes that matter today and kill or defer the rest. Protects deep work from a reactive job.
med: Three ranked bullets before starting work
highIntensity: Ranked top-3 plus explicit kill list
how:
1) Before deep work, list candidate tasks.
2) Force-rank to exactly three outcomes.
3) Explicitly kill or defer the rest.
4) Revisit only if a true emergency appears.

name: Ship one visible unit
description: Why: Ship something others can see: PR, doc, demo, or decision. Progress is shipped, not busy.
how:
1) Define a visible unit (PR, doc, demo, decision).
2) Time-box to finish something others can see.
3) Ship even if imperfect; open follow-ups separately.
4) Announce where stakeholders will notice.

name: Solicit hard feedback
description: Why: Ask for specific, critical feedback on a work product—not vague “how am I doing?”
highIntensity: Structured review of a work product with written takeaways
how:
1) Pick a specific work product.
2) Ask one person for hard, concrete feedback.
3) Write takeaways; change one behavior next week.
4) Thank them and close the loop.

name: Stakeholder comms batch
description: Why: Proactive status and risk updates in a batch so senior signal doesn’t require meetings all day.
highIntensity: Proactive status plus explicit risk callouts
how:
1) List stakeholders who need signal.
2) Send concise status: done / risk / next.
3) Call out risks early; do not hide bad news.
4) Batch updates so you are not in meetings all day.

name: Career-capital artifact
description: Why: Build optionality outside the current role: portfolio piece, OSS, talk outline, or public write-up.
med: 30 minutes on portfolio, OSS, or talk outline
how:
1) Choose portfolio, OSS, talk outline, or public note.
2) Work 30–90 min on something outside today’s ticket.
3) Leave a concrete artifact, not only “research.”
4) Aim to publish or present on a cadence.

name: Non-job creative practice
description: Why: Create in a domain that is not your job (music, drawing, writing, craft). Prevents pure-optimization identity collapse.
how:
1) Pick a non-job craft (music, drawing, writing, etc.).
2) Practice 20–60 min with no career KPI.
3) Make something small; finish a loop.
4) Protect the slot like a meeting.

name: Side project deep hour
description: Why: One focused hour on a side project with real stakes—often feeds career and intelligence without being pure work.
how:
1) Open the side project with one next action.
2) Deep block 30–120 min; no day-job tabs.
3) End with a commit, note, or demoable step.
4) Weekly is enough if intensity is real.

name: Unoptimized play
description: Why: Leisure with no productivity angle. Recovery for high-agency people who only “rest” productively.
how:
1) Schedule pure leisure with no self-improvement angle.
2) Do the fun thing without tracking it as “recovery protocol.”
3) Stop when the time is up or when you feel full.
4) Do not turn it into content or optimization.

name: Novel high-quality input
description: Why: Consume one high-quality novel input (film, essay, exhibit, album)—not doomscroll—to feed creativity.
med: One film, long essay, or exhibit
how:
1) Choose one high-quality film, essay, exhibit, or album.
2) Consume without multitasking doomscroll.
3) Optional: 5 bullets on what stuck.
4) Let it feed ideas; do not force productivity.

name: Make something for a person
description: Why: Make a small gift, tool, note, or artifact for a specific person. Creative + social dual hit; anti-isolation.
med: Small gift, note, or useful tool
how:
1) Pick a specific person.
2) Make a gift, note, tool, or helpful artifact for them.
3) Deliver it (send, give, ship).
4) Keep the bar human, not performative.

name: One-percent room upgrade
description: Why: Your environment quietly taxes attention and mood. Tiny daily upgrades compound into a space that supports the life you want—without a renovation project.
how:
1) Stand in the room and pick one friction: clutter, lighting, air, dirty surface, missing tool.
2) Spend 5–15 minutes improving only that (tidy one surface, open window, fix cable, put one thing away).
3) Stop when the timer ends—1% better is the win.
4) Optional: photo or one-line log so you see the compound curve.
med: 5 minutes: clear or fix one visible friction
highIntensity: 15–20 minutes deep tidy or one meaningful upgrade (lamp, storage, repair)

name: Reflect and write in full sentences
description: Why: Thoughts stay vague until language forces structure. Full-sentence writing turns fog into decisions, memory, and self-knowledge.
how:
1) Open a blank note (not chat).
2) Write 5–15 minutes in full sentences about what happened, what you think, or what you want.
3) No outline required; do not bullet-only.
4) End with one sentence: “So what I believe / will do is …”
highIntensity: 15–20 minutes free write plus a clear closing claim

name: Off before eleven
description: Why: Recovery and early starts are decided at night. Protecting the body with an early off-switch beats heroic mornings after late screens.
how:
1) Set a hard “systems off” time at or before 23:00 (screens, work, stimulating inputs).
2) Start wind-down 30–45 minutes earlier so off is realistic.
3) If you slip, do not spiral—resume the next night.
4) Pair with a fixed wake time so early start becomes default.
highIntensity: Full wind-down from 22:00; phone outside bedroom; consistent early wake

name: Attack an obvious problem
description: Why: Life fills with known, ignored frictions. Spending 30–60 minutes on something obvious builds agency—and you do not need to finish it today.
how:
1) Look around (home, work, health admin, relationships): list 2–3 “obvious” problems.
2) Pick one you have been avoiding.
3) Work 30–60 minutes doing something real about it (not just planning).
4) Stop on time even if unfinished; note the next physical action.
highIntensity: 60 minutes with a visible before/after or next-step artifact

name: Hypothesize, then validate
description: Why: Independent thinking is not hot takes—it is forming a clear hypothesis about how something works, then testing it against reality.
how:
1) Pick a system (code, market, person, process, body).
2) Write: “I think X works because Y.”
3) Design a small test: observe, measure, ask, experiment.
4) Update the hypothesis in writing: confirmed / revised / rejected.
highIntensity: Write hypothesis, run a deliberate test, document result

name: Open the conversation
description: Why: Connection rarely starts itself. Opening a conversation—and looking for help given or received—turns nearby people into a real network.
how:
1) Notice one person nearby (colleague, neighbor, acquaintance, online peer).
2) Open with a specific, low-pressure line (observation, question, appreciation).
3) Look for a way to help or a clean ask for help.
4) Leave the door open; do not force depth on first contact.
med: One genuine opener to one person
highIntensity: Conversation that includes a clear offer or ask

name: Happiness from help (self or others)
description: Why: Mood is more stable when ~80% of good feelings come from helping yourself or others—not only consumption or comparison. Reflection makes the pattern visible.
how:
1) When mood is good (or at day end), pause 2–5 minutes.
2) Write: what helped—help to self, help to others, or something else?
3) Aim to steer more of the day toward helpful action when possible.
4) Note one small helpful act for tomorrow if today was mostly passive pleasure.
med: One short reflection when mood is good
highIntensity: Daily log: sources of good mood + one deliberate helpful act

name: Categorize the day’s learning
description: Why: Learning without filing becomes noise. End-of-day categorization builds a personal knowledge system and reveals where growth actually happened.
how:
1) At day end, list 3–10 things you learned (facts, skills, people, self).
2) Sort into categories you reuse (e.g. work craft, people, health, money, self).
3) One line per item is enough.
4) Star anything that should change behavior tomorrow.
highIntensity: Full day dump + categories + one transfer action

name: Learn from standards you missed
description: Why: Rules and standards only help if misses become learning. Reviewing where you fell short builds integrity without shame spirals.
how:
1) List personal/professional rules or standards that mattered today.
2) Mark which you underperformed.
3) For each miss: what was the real cause (plan, energy, fear, environment)?
4) Write one concrete adjustment for next time—not a vague “try harder.”
highIntensity: Full review of key rules + written adjustments

name: Ask for help (let others help)
description: Why: Asking for help is not weakness—it gives others a chance to be useful and deepens bonds. Appreciation makes help sustainable.
how:
1) Name one stuck point where another person could help.
2) Ask specifically (what, by when, why them).
3) Make it easy to say yes or no.
4) Thank them and name that you appreciate them in your life—not only the task.
med: One clear ask to one person

name: Ask how you can do better
description: Why: Others see strengths and blind spots you cannot. Structured asks for improvement accelerate growth beyond self-assessment.
how:
1) Pick someone who observes your work or behavior.
2) Ask: “What’s one strength you see?” and “What’s one way I could do better next time?”
3) Listen without defending.
4) Write both answers; choose one improvement experiment for the next week.

name: Driver’s mindset
description: Why: In any activity, you are responsible for time, manner, and risk. Driver’s mindset is confident, observant, unhurried enough to do it right—without unnecessary risk.
how:
1) Before the activity, give yourself enough time (no heroic last-second squeeze).
2) State the goal and the non-negotiable safety/quality bounds.
3) Stay observant: environment, people, your own state.
4) Act with calm confidence; avoid unnecessary risk or rushed showboating.
med: One activity done with deliberate pace and scan
highIntensity: Plan time buffer + explicit risk check + debrief

name: Jokes, honesty, and stories
description: Why: Humor and honest storytelling make you memorable and human. Looking for the funny bit lightens life; telling how you see things builds connection.
how:
1) In conversation or writing, look for the funny or absurd angle—without cruelty.
2) Prefer honest stories over polished persona.
3) Tell how you actually see the situation in plain language.
4) One joke or one short story is enough; do not force a set.
med: One honest story or light joke in a real interaction
highIntensity: Write or tell a full story with a clear point of view

name: Love with care
description: Why: Passion without care becomes self-centered. Loving deeper means tracking others’ well-being—not only your intensity of feeling.
how:
1) Pick someone you care about.
2) Ask (or notice): what would support their well-being today?
3) Act on care—time, help, listening, protection—not only romantic or self-focused passion.
4) Check impact: did they feel considered, or only pursued?
med: One care-first action for one person
highIntensity: Deep conversation or substantial support focused on their needs

name: Morning outdoor light
description: Why: Early bright light (ideally outdoor) sets circadian clocks, supports daytime alertness and nighttime sleep pressure—core Huberman circadian protocol.
how:
1) Within ~30–60 min of waking, get outdoor light (no sunglasses if safe).
2) Aim ~10 min bright day / ~20–30 min cloudy.
3) Do not stare at the sun; face general outdoor brightness.
4) If you wake before sunrise, use bright indoor light then go outside after dawn.

name: Delay caffeine 90–120 min
description: Why: Waiting 90–120 minutes after waking lets adenosine clear and cortisol peak settle; often reduces mid-morning crash (Huberman caffeine timing protocol).
how:
1) Note wake time.
2) No caffeine for 90–120 minutes.
3) Hydrate; use light and movement for early alertness.
4) Then take caffeine if desired; cut off ~8–10 h before bed.

name: Physiological double sigh
description: Why: Two inhales through the nose + long exhale through the mouth rapidly reduces autonomic arousal—fast stress tool from Huberman / Feldman research.
how:
1) Inhale fully through the nose.
2) Sip a second short inhale to fully inflate lungs.
3) Long slow exhale through the mouth until empty.
4) Repeat 1–3 cycles when stressed or before sleep.

name: NSDR / Yoga Nidra
description: Why: Non-sleep deep rest restores dopamine and recovery without a full nap; Huberman often recommends NSDR after learning or poor sleep.
how:
1) Lie down; use a NSDR or Yoga Nidra audio (10–30 min).
2) Stay still; follow body scan / breath cues.
3) If you fall asleep, fine—still useful.
4) Use after deep work, training, or sleep debt days.

name: Zone-2 cardio (Huberman)
description: Why: Sustained easy aerobic work supports mitochondrial and cardiovascular health; Huberman commonly cites ~150–200 min/week Zone 2 as a backbone.
how:
1) Choose walk, jog, bike, row at conversational pace.
2) Stay nasal-breathing easy or able to speak sentences.
3) Build toward multi-session weekly total (not one redline day).
4) Separate from hard intervals when possible.

name: Resistance training bout
description: Why: Progressive resistance supports muscle, metabolism, bone, and neuromodulators; Huberman frames strength work as non-negotiable for long-term healthspan.
how:
1) Train major patterns (squat/hinge/push/pull/carry) 2–4×/week.
2) Leave 1–3 reps in reserve; progress load or reps over weeks.
3) Warm up joints; control eccentrics.
4) Sleep and protein support adaptation.

name: Evening dim / low overhead light
description: Why: Bright overhead and blue-heavy light at night suppresses melatonin and shifts clocks late; dim, low lamps protect sleep timing.
how:
1) After sunset, reduce overhead LEDs.
2) Prefer lamps, warm light, lower screens brightness.
3) If screens are required, dim + distance; consider blue reduction late.
4) Keep bedroom dark for sleep.
highIntensity: Full wind-down lighting from 2–3 h before bed

name: Deliberate cold exposure
description: Why: Brief cold (shower/plunge) can raise alertness and resilience to stress; Huberman discusses cold as a deliberate stressor with recovery benefits when dosed sanely.
how:
1) End shower with 1–3 min cool/cold, or short plunge.
2) Breathe calm; do not hyperventilate dangerously in water.
3) 2–4×/week is enough for most; avoid forcing if ill.
4) Not a substitute for sleep or training basics.
highIntensity: 2–3 minutes cold plunge or long cold shower

name: Deliberate heat (sauna)
description: Why: Repeated heat exposure is linked with cardiovascular and recovery benefits in the literature Huberman cites; use heat as a deliberate protocol, not ego endurance.
how:
1) Sauna or hot bath in safe ranges for your health status.
2) Typical pattern discussed: multiple rounds/week, not extreme one-offs.
3) Hydrate; exit if dizzy; medical clearance if needed.
4) Pair with cool-down; avoid right before late sleep if it impairs you.

name: 90-minute focus bout
description: Why: Ultradian ~90-minute deep work matches natural alertness cycles; Huberman emphasizes phone-free focus then rest/NSDR.
how:
1) Define one cognitive outcome.
2) Phone out of room; notifications off.
3) Work ~90 minutes (or 50–90 if building up).
4) Then deliberate rest: walk, NSDR, or soft eyes—not more doomscroll.

name: Post-meal walk
description: Why: Light walking after meals improves glucose disposal and aids digestion/alertness; simple high-ROI protocol Huberman often endorses.
how:
1) After a main meal, walk 5–30 minutes easy.
2) Outdoor light is a bonus.
3) Keep it conversational; not a workout substitute.
4) Consistency beats duration.

name: No phone first 60–90 min
description: Why: Early high-dopamine phone use spikes then flattens motivation; Huberman advises delaying phone to protect morning dopamine baseline.
how:
1) Wake without opening social/email apps.
2) Light, move, hydrate, plan first.
3) First phone use after 60–90 minutes (or after key morning block).
4) Put phone to charge outside reach overnight if needed.

name: Panoramic / distance vision breaks
description: Why: Long hours of near focus (screens) stress the visual system; outdoor panoramic vision and distance gazes support eye comfort and circadian light entry.
how:
1) Every 20–30 min of near work, look far for 20–30+ seconds.
2) Get outdoor distance viewing daily when possible.
3) Soften gaze; avoid constant “tunnel” screen posture.
4) Combine with morning outdoor light protocol.

name: Learn then deliberate rest
description: Why: Skill and knowledge stick better when deep encoding is followed by rest/NSDR rather than immediate distraction—Huberman learning protocol theme.
how:
1) Do a focused learning block (reading, skill, language).
2) Immediately after: 10–20 min NSDR, quiet walk, or eyes-closed rest.
3) Avoid switching to high-dopamine phone content right after.
4) Space repetitions across days.

name: Quality social connection
description: Why: Real social connection is a major neuromodulator and healthspan factor; Huberman discusses relationships as biological, not optional soft skills.
how:
1) Schedule or seize one real connection (call, meal, walk).
2) Prefer presence over performative networking.
3) Listen; share something real.
4) Protect recurring high-quality ties weekly.

name: Sleep schedule consistency
description: Why: Consistent sleep/wake timing is among the highest-ROI levers Huberman emphasizes for mood, hormones, and cognition.
how:
1) Fix a wake time (including weekends ±30–60 min max).
2) Back-calculate bedtime for sufficient duration.
3) Protect wind-down; same cue sequence nightly.
4) Use morning light to anchor the schedule.
highIntensity: Fixed wake + fixed bedtime including weekends

name: Morning movement for alertness
description: Why: Light + movement after waking raises body temperature and alertness; Huberman pairs outdoor walking with circadian light exposure.
how:
1) After wake, move: walk, mobility, or easy calisthenics.
2) Prefer outdoor for light combo.
3) 5–30 minutes; not a max workout.
4) Then deep work or delayed caffeine window.

name: Cyclic sighing practice
description: Why: Brief daily cyclic sighing improved mood in peer-reviewed work Huberman has highlighted; a structured daily breath practice beats ad-hoc only.
how:
1) Sit or stand tall.
2) For 5 minutes: repeated physiological double sighs (or guided cyclic sighing).
3) Same time daily if possible (e.g. afternoon stress peak).
4) Track mood/energy subjectively.

highIntensity: Full ~90 minutes + notes of what failed
name: Ultradian learning block
description: Why: Huberman frames deep learning in ~90-minute ultradian bouts of focused encoding, then rest—matching natural alertness cycles.
how:
1) Pick one skill/topic.
2) Work 50–90 minutes with phone away.
3) Stay with productive struggle; minimize tab-switching.
4) End the block deliberately; then rest or NSDR.

name: Retrieval practice
description: Why: Testing yourself beats re-reading for durable memory—core learning science Huberman emphasizes for neuroplasticity.
how:
1) Close notes/book.
2) Write or speak everything you can recall.
3) Check gaps; re-encode only misses.
4) Repeat across days (spacing).

med: 15 minutes hard practice with errors allowed
name: Error-driven learning
description: Why: Errors + attention release neuromodulators that open plasticity; Huberman stresses leaning into mistakes rather than only easy success.
how:
1) Choose a drill slightly above comfort.
2) Attempt before peeking at answers.
3) Mark each error without shame.
4) Correct immediately; log one pattern of mistakes.

name: Teach-back / explain aloud
description: Why: Generation and teaching force deeper encoding; Huberman often recommends explaining material in plain language to lock learning.
how:
1) After a learning bout, explain the idea out loud or on paper as if teaching a smart novice.
2) No jargon crutches.
3) Note where explanation breaks—those are gaps.
4) Optionally record a 3-minute voice note.

name: Spaced repetition pass
description: Why: Spacing beats massed cramming for long-term retention—Huberman cites sleep + spaced re-exposure as plasticity multipliers.
how:
1) Revisit material from 1+ days ago (not only today’s).
2) Use cards, summary, or re-solve problems.
3) Prioritize weak items.
4) Keep sessions short and frequent.

med: Protect sleep after any major learning day
highIntensity: Full consistent schedule + NSDR if short
name: Sleep same day as hard learning
description: Why: Sleep consolidates learning; Huberman stresses not sacrificing night sleep after intense study or skill practice.
how:
1) Schedule hard learning earlier enough to protect bedtime.
2) Avoid all-nighters after encoding.
3) If sleep-deprived, use NSDR and re-learn later—don’t stack debt.
4) Log: learning day → target sleep window held.

highIntensity: 2 minutes deliberate visual focus then work
name: Visual focus spotlight
description: Why: Narrowing visual attention (staring at a target) can increase mental focus; Huberman links ocular focus to cognitive focus.
how:
1) Before deep work, pick a visual target at arm’s length or on screen edge.
2) Hold soft, steady gaze 30–60 seconds.
3) Then begin the cognitive task.
4) If mind drifts, briefly re-anchor gaze and return.

name: Interleaved practice
description: Why: Mixing related skills (interleaving) often beats blocked drills for transfer—advanced learning protocol aligned with plasticity research Huberman discusses.
how:
1) Pick 2–3 related sub-skills.
2) Rotate short bouts rather than one skill for the whole session.
3) Keep difficulty high enough to make errors.
4) End with 2-minute summary of patterns.

name: Try before answer (generation)
description: Why: Attempting retrieval or solution before seeing the answer strengthens encoding—the generation effect Huberman-aligned learning science supports.
how:
1) Cover the solution.
2) Produce your best attempt first.
3) Only then reveal and correct.
4) Note the delta in one line.

name: Handwrite key notes
description: Why: Handwriting can improve processing versus pure typing for some learners; Huberman often encourages analog capture during learning bouts.
how:
1) During or after learning, write main ideas by hand.
2) Use full phrases, not only doodles.
3) Limit to one page.
4) Optional photo archive later.

name: Undistracted mind-wander walk
description: Why: Default-mode mind-wandering supports creative insight; Huberman often recommends walks without podcasts/phone for idea generation.
how:
1) Walk 10–30 minutes.
2) No podcast, no scrolling, no calls.
3) Let thoughts roam; optionally capture one idea at the end.
4) Outdoor if possible.

name: Create before cheap dopamine
description: Why: Morning dopamine baseline is fragile; Huberman advises delaying phone/social so early creative or hard work isn’t undercut by cheap rewards.
how:
1) After light/move, do 20–45 minutes of creative or hard make-work.
2) Phone still offline or in another room.
3) Define one output (sketch, draft, riff, design).
4) Only then open messages if needed.

name: NSDR after creative struggle
description: Why: NSDR after effort can support consolidation and insight; Huberman links non-sleep deep rest to learning and mental reset useful for creative work.
how:
1) Do a hard creative bout first.
2) Immediately do 10–20 min NSDR/Yoga Nidra.
3) Capture any ideas that surface after.
4) Don’t replace night sleep with NSDR.

name: Deliberate novelty input
description: Why: Novelty stimulates neuromodulators and creative recombination; Huberman discusses new experiences as fuel—not endless scrolling.
how:
1) Pick one novel but high-quality input (place, genre, technique, person).
2) Engage 20–40 minutes with attention.
3) Note one connection to your work.
4) Avoid passive doomscroll as “novelty.”

name: Single-context create block
description: Why: Context switching burns focus and dopamine; Huberman’s focus protocols favor one cognitive context at a time for quality output.
how:
1) One creative project only for the block.
2) Close other docs/chats.
3) 25–50 minutes uninterrupted.
4) Batch admin after, not during.

name: Goal-free play bout
description: Why: Play without optimization supports creativity and recovery from goal-stacking—aligned with Huberman themes on balancing effort and reward.
how:
1) Pick play with no KPI (instrument, sketch, game of pure fun).
2) Set a timer 15–30 minutes.
3) No recording for “content.”
4) Stop when timer ends.

med: Nasal default for easy activity only
name: Nasal breathing default
description: Why: Huberman often recommends nasal breathing at rest and during easy exercise for airway health, nitric oxide, and calmer autonomic tone.
how:
1) Keep mouth closed during easy walks/desk work when comfortable.
2) If congested, gentle clear; don’t force through pain.
3) During hard intervals, mouth may open—return to nose in recovery.
4) Check-in 3× daily: am I mouth-breathing unnecessively?

name: Long-exhale calm set
description: Why: Longer exhales bias parasympathetic tone; Huberman teaches exhale-emphasized breathing to reduce stress quickly.
how:
1) Inhale calmly through nose ~3–4 s.
2) Exhale longer ~6–8 s through nose or pursed lips.
3) Repeat 5–10 cycles.
4) Use before sleep or after stress spikes.

name: Box breathing set
description: Why: Equal-count box breathing is a simple Huberman-adjacent focus/calm tool for steadying arousal before performance.
how:
1) Inhale 4 counts, hold 4, exhale 4, hold 4 (adjust length to comfort).
2) Repeat 4–8 boxes.
3) Sit upright; nasal preferred.
4) Use pre-meeting or pre-deep-work.

med: Use at least once on a real spike
highIntensity: Use on every noticed spike that day
name: Physiological sigh on stress spike
description: Why: Real-time use of the double inhale + long exhale when stress hits—Huberman’s go-to acute anxiety tool (distinct from scheduled cyclic sighing practice).
how:
1) Notice spike (email, conflict, rumination).
2) Immediately: double nasal inhale + long mouth exhale ×1–3.
3) Resume task only after one clear breath.
4) Optional log of triggers.

name: CO₂ tolerance walk
description: Why: Comfort with elevated CO₂ relates to calm under stress; Huberman discusses nasal/exhale training and controlled breath holds in safe contexts (never forced underwater).
how:
1) Easy walk, nasal only.
2) Occasionally extend exhale comfort—not to dizziness.
3) Stop if lightheaded.
4) 5–15 minutes total.

highIntensity: Up to 3 rounds, fully recovered between
name: Cyclic hyperventilation (safe dose)
description: Why: Huberman discusses cyclic hyperventilation (Wim Hof–like) for adrenaline; use sparingly, seated/lying, never near water, stop if unsafe—advanced voluntary stressor.
how:
1) Sit or lie down safely (not in water/driving).
2) 25–30 deep breaths, then exhale and hold comfortably empty until urge to breathe.
3) Recover breath; 1–3 rounds max.
4) Skip if pregnant, seizure history, or unwell; this is optional advanced.

name: Pre-sleep physiological sighs
description: Why: Slow breathing and physiological sighs before bed can downshift arousal—part of Huberman’s sleep toolkit when mind is racing.
how:
1) Lights dim; in bed or chair.
2) 5–10 physiological double sighs or long-exhale sets.
3) No phone during the set.
4) Transition to sleep without rechecking screens.

highIntensity: All major rewards gated behind effort
name: Effort before reward
description: Why: Huberman’s dopamine framework: random/cheap rewards blunt motivation; put effort first, then deliberate reward.
how:
1) Name the hard effort block first.
2) Complete it before preferred treat (snack, episode, social scroll).
3) Keep reward proportional—not a binge.
4) One clear effort→reward chain per day minimum.

med: Skip reward on one completed micro-task
name: Intermittent (not constant) reward
description: Why: Constant reward predictability flattens dopamine peaks; Huberman advises intermittent celebration of wins.
how:
1) Do not reward every micro-task.
2) After a meaningful win, sometimes celebrate, sometimes just log and continue.
3) Avoid stacking layers of rewards for one task.
4) Weekly: one deliberate celebration only.

name: Low-dopamine morning window
description: Why: Protecting morning from stacked stimulants/social media preserves motivation—Huberman dopamine baseline protocol.
how:
1) First 60–120 min: no social feeds, no junk video, minimal novelty apps.
2) Light, move, hydrate, work or create.
3) Caffeine delayed if that’s your rule.
4) Open high-dopamine apps only after the window.

name: Cold for long dopamine tone
description: Why: Deliberate cold can elevate dopamine for hours in studied protocols Huberman cites—use as a mood/motivation tool, not punishment.
how:
1) Uncomfortably cold but safe exposure (shower finish or immersion).
2) 1–3+ minutes depending on tolerance; build weekly minutes.
3) Breathe calmly; never hyperventilate in water.
4) Prefer morning/midday if it disrupts sleep.

med: One reframe on a real stressor
name: Stress-is-enhancing reframe
description: Why: Huberman discusses stress mindset: brief reappraisal (“this stress can enhance me”) changes physiology versus pure threat framing.
how:
1) When stress hits, name it out loud or on paper.
2) Add: “This can sharpen me for X.”
3) Take one action aligned with that frame.
4) Avoid toxic positivity—acknowledge difficulty first.

name: Specific gratitude (story form)
description: Why: Huberman notes story-based, specific gratitude (not generic lists) can shift autonomic state and social neuromodulators.
how:
1) Recall a specific person/event that helped you.
2) Write 5–8 sentences of the story and how it felt.
3) Optionally thank them.
4) Prefer depth over a long shallow list.

name: Near–far focus drills
description: Why: Huberman’s vision toolkit includes accommodation practice—shifting focus near to far to train flexible focusing.
how:
1) Hold a thumb or pen at mid-distance; focus 5 s.
2) Shift to a far target 5 s.
3) Repeat 10–20 cycles.
4) Relax eyes after; blink fully.

name: Smooth pursuit eye tracking
description: Why: Smooth pursuit exercises appear in Huberman vision protocols to train coordinated eye movements.
how:
1) Slowly move a thumb left–right and up–down at arm’s length.
2) Eyes track without jumping; head mostly still.
3) 1–2 minutes.
4) Stop if strain; blink and rest.

highIntensity: Full morning light walk unsunglassed when safe
name: Morning light without sunglasses
description: Why: For circadian setting, Huberman generally recommends outdoor light to the eyes without sunglasses (when safe) in the morning protocol.
how:
1) Morning outdoor light session.
2) Skip sunglasses unless medically required or unsafe glare.
3) Never stare at the sun.
4) Use hat for comfort if needed while still getting outdoor lux.

highIntensity: Every 20 minutes during deep work day
name: Complete blink breaks
description: Why: Screen work reduces blink quality; Huberman vision hygiene includes deliberate full blinks to keep eyes comfortable and focused longer.
how:
1) Every 20 minutes of screens: 10 slow full blinks.
2) Soften forehead and jaw.
3) Optional 20-second far gaze after.
4) Increase humidity/blink if dry.

med: One room switched to dim warm light
name: Red/amber lamp last hours
description: Why: Lower short-wavelength light at night protects melatonin; Huberman often suggests dim red/amber lighting late evening.
how:
1) Last 1–2 hours before bed: switch to lamps, prefer warm/red/amber.
2) Kill bright overheads.
3) Dim screens or use night modes as backup—not a full substitute for dim rooms.
4) Bedroom dark for sleep.

name: Midday outdoor light dose
description: Why: Additional daytime outdoor light reinforces circadian amplitude and mood—Huberman circadian toolkit beyond only morning light.
how:
1) Get outside around midday or early afternoon 5–15 minutes.
2) Combine with walk or post-meal stroll.
3) No need to stare at sun.
4) Cloudy still counts—longer if dim.

name: VO₂ max / sprint bout
description: Why: Huberman’s foundational fitness includes periodic high-intensity work for VO₂ max alongside Zone 2 and strength.
how:
1) Fully warm up.
2) 1–6 hard intervals (e.g. 20–60 s hard, full recover) as appropriate for your level.
3) Stop if form or chest pain issues—medical clearance if needed.
4) 1×/week is enough for many.

med: No max-intensity training in last 2–3 h before bed
highIntensity: All hard training finished by mid-afternoon
name: Exercise timing for sleep
description: Why: Hard training late can delay sleep for some; Huberman discusses placing intense exercise earlier when sleep is a priority.
how:
1) If sleep suffers, move hard sessions earlier in the day.
2) Keep late movement easy (walk, mobility).
3) Track sleep quality vs training time one week.
4) Adjust based on your data, not dogma.

med: Finish main meal ≥2 h before bed most nights
highIntensity: Strict 3 h buffer + earlier digestion walk
name: Last meal buffer before bed
description: Why: Huberman often suggests finishing large meals ~2–3 hours before sleep for sleep quality and metabolism (individual variation applies).
how:
1) Set a kitchen cutoff time aligned to bedtime.
2) Prefer smaller earlier dinner if reflux/sleep issues.
3) Hydrate earlier; sip only late if needed.
4) Flexibility for social life—optimize most nights.

highIntensity: Planned high-protein breakfast within eating window
name: Protein-forward first meal
description: Why: Huberman discusses protein distribution and daytime eating patterns supporting muscle and satiety—practical first-meal structure.
how:
1) Include a clear protein source in first real meal.
2) Pair with whole foods; don’t only liquid sugar.
3) Eat after morning light when possible.
4) Note energy/cravings until lunch.

name: Neck & posture micro-set
description: Why: Huberman has highlighted neck training/posture for resilience and desk health as part of a complete physical protocol.
how:
1) Gentle neck mobility through pain-free ranges.
2) Optional light isometric holds if trained for it.
3) Open chest after screens.
4) 3–5 minutes; never force cervical joints.

name: Heat after training (optional)
description: Why: Huberman discusses sauna/heat often after training in studied patterns; optional recovery/heat-shock protein stimulus when healthy enough.
how:
1) After strength or cardio (not if overheating/ill).
2) Sauna or hot bath in safe durations.
3) Hydrate; exit if dizzy.
4) Avoid very late heat if it impairs your sleep.

name: Focused-attention meditation
description: Why: Huberman covers meditation types; focused attention (breath/anchor) trains concentration circuits complementary to open monitoring.
how:
1) Sit 5–13 minutes.
2) Anchor on breath or spot.
3) When mind wanders, note and return—no self-attack.
4) Same time daily if possible.

name: Open monitoring meditation
description: Why: Open monitoring builds awareness of thoughts/feelings without fixation—another Huberman-discussed meditation family for emotional flexibility.
how:
1) Sit 5–13 minutes.
2) Observe sounds, body, thoughts arising/passing.
3) Don’t chase or suppress.
4) End with one breath of orientation to the room.

name: Self-hypnosis / Reverie bout
description: Why: Huberman has discussed clinical hypnosis and tools like self-hypnosis for focus, sleep, and habit change as a distinct state from meditation.
how:
1) Use a reputable self-hypnosis script or app protocol.
2) 10–15 minutes undisturbed.
3) Pick one target (sleep, focus, calm).
4) Don’t drive/operate machinery during.

name: Accountability declaration
description: Why: Huberman notes social accountability can increase follow-through on focus and goals via externalized commitment.
how:
1) Tell a specific person your next hard block or habit target.
2) Include when you’ll report back.
3) Keep the ask small and concrete.
4) Close the loop with a result message.

name: Caffeine cutoff 8–10 h before bed
description: Why: Sleep toolkit staple from Huberman: stop caffeine ~8–10 hours before target sleep to protect sleep architecture.
how:
1) Back-calculate cutoff from bedtime.
2) Switch to non-caffeinated options after.
3) Watch hidden caffeine (tea, soda, preworkout).
4) If sensitive, extend buffer.

highIntensity: Water + electrolytes + no caffeine until hydrated
name: Morning hydrate (electrolytes optional)
description: Why: Huberman often mentions hydrating on waking (sometimes with electrolytes) to support alertness and replace overnight fluid loss.
how:
1) On waking, drink a full glass of water before caffeine.
2) Optional pinch of electrolytes if you sweat/caffeine heavily—don’t overdo salt if contraindicated.
3) Pair with morning light.
4) Continue steady hydration daytime.

name: Net-worth snapshot
description: Why: Tracking net worth (assets − liabilities) is a simple, evidence-aligned way to see whether wealth is actually compounding—not just income vibes.
how:
1) Update balances: cash, investments, debts, major assets (rough is fine).
2) Record net worth and date.
3) Note one driver of change (saved, markets, debt paydown, spend).
4) No daily obsessing—weekly or monthly cadence.

highIntensity: Raise contribution rate or fix a broken auto-invest
name: Auto-invest confirmation
description: Why: Automated contributions to diversified investments beat timing the market for most people; checking the pipe runs prevents silent failure.
how:
1) Confirm scheduled transfers to investment/retirement accounts executed.
2) If cash piled up, increase automation or invest the surplus per your rule.
3) Prefer broad low-cost funds unless you have a written reason otherwise.
4) Log “ran / fixed.”

highIntensity: Full month calc + plan to lift rate 1–2 points
name: Savings-rate check
description: Why: Savings rate (saved ÷ income) strongly predicts wealth building more than stock-picking skill for typical households.
how:
1) Estimate this month’s income and amount saved/invested.
2) Compute rough savings rate.
3) If below your target, cut one spend or raise income action.
4) Write the target rate somewhere visible.

med: Minimum + small extra to highest APR
highIntensity: Aggressive extra payment + cut the spending source
name: High-interest debt attack
description: Why: Paying down high-APR debt is often a guaranteed high “return”; evidence favors prioritizing costly consumer debt.
how:
1) List debts with APRs.
2) Extra payment to highest APR (or snowball if adherence needs wins).
3) Avoid new high-interest balances.
4) Log payment made.

highIntensity: Rebuild runway plan with automatic transfers
name: Cash runway check
description: Why: Emergency liquidity reduces forced selling and panic; runway in months/weeks of essential expenses is a standard resilience metric.
how:
1) Essential monthly burn estimate.
2) Liquid cash ÷ burn = runway.
3) If thin, route surplus to cash before aggressive risk.
4) Target a runway band you pre-chose (e.g. 3–6 months).

name: Lifestyle-creep intercept
description: Why: Income rises often get eaten by lifestyle; intercepting upgrades preserves savings rate—the main wealth lever.
how:
1) Notice one recent or tempting upgrade (housing, car, subscription, dining).
2) Ask: does this raise long-term options or only status?
3) Delay 72 hours or set a cheaper default.
4) Route the difference to invest/debt.

name: Income-skill deliberate hour
description: Why: Human capital and scarce skills drive lifetime earnings more than frugality alone; invest hours in monetizable skill.
how:
1) Pick one skill with market demand (craft, sales, systems, credential).
2) 45–90 minutes deliberate practice or portfolio proof.
3) Ship a visible artifact when possible.
4) Track hours monthly.

highIntensity: Full prep + send the ask or book the meeting
name: Compensation negotiation prep
description: Why: Negotiation and market data move total compensation; small percentage gains compound across a career.
how:
1) Gather 1–2 market data points for your role.
2) Write your value bullets and ask range.
3) Practice the script once aloud.
4) Schedule or take one real step (doc, chat, application).

highIntensity: Increase contribution or open missing account
name: Tax-advantaged account check
description: Why: Using tax-advantaged accounts (when available) improves after-tax compounding—standard evidence-based advice.
how:
1) Confirm contribution room / employer match status.
2) Capture match first if offered.
3) Increase auto % if under-using room and cashflow allows.
4) One note: “match free money: yes/no.”

highIntensity: Full week of schedule-only portfolio actions
name: No market-timing decision
description: Why: For most investors, time in market beats timing; a weekly habit to refuse impulsive trades protects long-run returns.
how:
1) Notice urge to trade on news/fear/greed.
2) Default: do nothing; stick to IPS/auto plan.
3) If changing strategy, wait 48 hours and write reasons.
4) Log “no impulsive trade.”

name: Personal unit economics
description: Why: Knowing cost per useful unit (commute meal, subscription hour of joy, side-project hourly) improves decisions like a simple business case.
how:
1) Pick one recurring spend.
2) Estimate cost per use or per hour of value.
3) Keep, cut, or renegotiate based on the number.
4) Write the unit cost down.

name: Learn one money concept
description: Why: Financial literacy compounds decisions; short, accurate learning (index funds, fees, inflation, risk) beats hot tips.
how:
1) Pick one concept (fees, inflation, diversification, tax basics).
2) Read/watch a high-quality source 15–25 minutes.
3) Write a 5-sentence explanation in your words.
4) Note one behavior change if any.

name: Single-task sprint
description: Why: Multitasking taxes working memory and raises subjective stress while lowering quality; single-task sprints keep calm focus.
how:
1) One task only for 25–50 minutes.
2) Notifications off; one window.
3) If interrupted, park the interrupt on paper.
4) Short break after—no feed spiral.

name: Worry dump then close
description: Why: Externalizing worries reduces rumination loops; closing the list returns attention to the present task—calm with readiness.
how:
1) Set 5–10 minutes.
2) Write every open loop/worry uncensored.
3) Star only items actionable today; schedule or trash the rest.
4) Physically close the note and start one action or one breath set.

name: Alert-calm body reset
description: Why: Soft eyes, longer exhales, and relaxed jaw/shoulders lower arousal without sleepiness—body state for sharp work under pressure.
how:
1) Drop shoulders; unclench jaw.
2) Soften gaze (wider peripheral).
3) 5 long exhales.
4) Return to task with one clear next action.

highIntensity: Zero feeds outside a single 20-minute slot
name: Info-diet window
description: Why: Constant news/feeds raise anxiety and fragment attention; a bounded info window keeps you informed without ambient stress.
how:
1) Pick one or two windows/day for news/social.
2) Outside windows: no feeds.
3) Prefer written summaries over rage video.
4) End window on a timer.

name: Calm premortem
description: Why: Premortems reduce anxiety from ambiguity by converting vague dread into specific risks and mitigations—sharp planning without panic.
how:
1) Name the upcoming decision/event.
2) “It’s 3 months later and it failed—why?” list 5 reasons.
3) Add one mitigation each.
4) Stop at timebox; act on top mitigation only.

highIntensity: All caffeine doses paired with written outcomes
name: Caffeine only with a focus plan
description: Why: Caffeine amplifies arousal—pair with a written focus target so it sharpens work instead of sharpening anxiety and tab-hopping.
how:
1) Before caffeine, write the one outcome for the next block.
2) Consume caffeine.
3) Start the block within 10 minutes.
4) No caffeine as boredom entertainment.

name: Capture one mental model
description: Why: Building toward ~100 models starts with deliberate capture—name, definition, domain—so models become reusable tools, not vibes.
how:
1) Encounter or recall one model (e.g. opportunity cost, inversion, base rates).
2) Write: name, 2–3 sentence definition, one example.
3) Tag domain (biz, mind, systems, people).
4) Store in a single running list/deck.

highIntensity: Two models applied to same decision + pick
name: Apply a model to a real decision
description: Why: Models only pay rent when applied; force one model onto a live decision to train transfer.
how:
1) Pick a real decision today.
2) Choose one model from your list.
3) Write how the model changes the analysis or choice.
4) Decide or note the open question.

name: Inversion pass
description: Why: Inversion (“what would guarantee failure?”) is a core Munger-style model that surfaces risks and stupidity avoidance.
how:
1) State the goal.
2) List ways to fail guaranteed.
3) Avoid those paths explicitly.
4) Convert top failures into checklists.

highIntensity: Map three branches two levels deep
name: Second-order consequences
description: Why: First-order thinking is common; second-order (“and then what?”) is a foundational model for strategy and personal choices.
how:
1) State the action.
2) Write first-order effects.
3) For each, write second-order effects (and then…).
4) Adjust action if second-order is ugly.

med: One decision with explicit base-rate note
highIntensity: Base rate + comparison class research 20 min
name: Base-rate before story
description: Why: Outside view / base rates beat narrative bias; check reference classes before vivid stories decide for you.
how:
1) Frame the prediction or bet.
2) Ask: what’s the base rate for similar cases?
3) Only then weigh the unique story.
4) Write both numbers/story and the adjusted view.

med: One yes with named opportunity cost
highIntensity: Audit three commitments with opportunity costs
name: Name the opportunity cost
description: Why: Every yes is a no to something else; naming opportunity cost is a high-ROI model for time and money.
how:
1) State the commitment (time/money).
2) Write the next-best alternative sacrificed.
3) Keep only if still worth it.
4) Optional: estimate hours or dollars of the alternative.

name: Feynman a model
description: Why: If you can’t explain a model simply, you don’t own it; Feynman technique builds a real latticework, not name-dropping.
how:
1) Pick one model from your list.
2) Explain it in plain language without jargon.
3) Mark gaps; re-study only gaps.
4) Add a sharper example.

name: Spaced review of model deck
description: Why: A path to ~100 models requires spaced review or the latticework decays into trivia.
how:
1) Open your model list/deck.
2) Review 5–15 models: define + example from memory.
3) Fail → rewrite card.
4) Prefer weak cards.

highIntensity: Two mappings + present one to someone
name: Cross-domain model transfer
description: Why: Latticework means borrowing models across domains (biology→business, physics→product); transfer is the advanced skill.
how:
1) Pick a model from domain A.
2) Force-apply to a problem in domain B (work, health, relationships).
3) Write what transfers and what breaks.
4) Keep the valid mapping in your deck.

name: Kill or update a bad model
description: Why: Wrong models are worse than none; Bayesian updating / killing pet theories keeps the lattice honest.
how:
1) Find a belief/model you use that failed recently.
2) Write disconfirming evidence.
3) Revise or retire it explicitly.
4) Note the replacement rule.

name: Read from a model source
description: Why: Quality inputs (clear thinkers, model catalogs, case studies) feed the path to a large, accurate set of mental models.
how:
1) Read 15–30 minutes from a high-signal source on reasoning/models/cases.
2) Extract one model or sharpen an existing one.
3) Capture to your deck.
4) Avoid hot-take threads as primary source.

med: One decision tagged in/out of circle
highIntensity: Map three active projects to the circle
name: Circle of competence check
description: Why: Knowing the edge of what you understand prevents overconfident bets—classic model for career and investing.
how:
1) For a live opinion or bet, draw: core competence / edge / outside.
2) Mark where this decision sits.
3) If outside, get help, shrink size, or learn first.
4) Write one humility constraint.
